idiom_name: Map of handlers with an explicit fallback, swapped as a whole on rule reload
implementation_notes: Node.js has no router abstraction, so the rule base is a Map (or a null-prototype object) from routing key to handler function and the control channel is whatever mutates it - a watcher that re-evaluates the rules module after clearing the require cache, or an admin endpoint calling table.set. Two hazards are JavaScript-specific: a missing key yields undefined and calling it throws inside the message loop, so the fallback must be explicit, and Map.set is synchronously visible to the event loop, so a multi-rule update must build the new table first and publish it in one step rather than mutating entry by entry across awaits. For event-shaped traffic an EventEmitter does the same job by swapping listeners (removeListener/addListener).
pitfalls: Mutating entries one at a time while messages are in flight routes some messages by the old and some by the new rule set; build then swap.
require() caches modules, so editing the rules file changes nothing until the cache entry is deleted (delete require.cache[require.resolve('./rules')]) - or the process restarts.
An unhandled missing handler is a TypeError inside the message loop that can take the consumer down; always default to an explicit dead-letter handler.
Async handlers that capture a table reference keep the previous generation alive and delay collection of stale rule closures.
